payload.title: Bridesmaids Tradition and Where It Comes From
payload.excerpt: Why do we have bridesmaids? From the wedding feasts of classical Athens to Queen Victoria's twelve in white: maid or matron of honour, how many to ask, bridesmen, thanking your attendants, and asking friends to travel for a destination wedding.
key_takeaways: We have bridesmaids so a bride has people she trusts beside her, helping before and during the ceremony, with the maid of honour leading them.
Queen Victoria had twelve bridesmaids in 1840, all eldest daughters of peers, dressed in white to her own design.
Traditionally, bridesmaids received a piece of jewellery, such as a brooch or locket, as a gift or souvenir of the wedding.
For a wedding abroad, ask attendants early and talk openly about travel, time off and who covers what before anyone books.

faq.a: To help the bride before and during the ceremony, and to stand with her through the day. Weddings in classical Athens and Rome had attendants too.

faq.q: What is the difference between a maid of honour and a matron of honour?
faq.a: The maid of honour is the most important bridesmaid. A matron of honour is a married woman in the same lead role. The duties are the same.

faq.q: Is it okay to have no bridesmaids?
faq.a: Yes. Many couples marry with one attendant or none, especially at a small ceremony abroad. A sibling or friend can still hold the rings and stand beside you.

faq.q: Can a man be a bridesmaid?
faq.a: Yes. A bridesman takes on the same role on the bride's side, and many couples now have mixed wedding parties.

faq.q: Do bridesmaids have to travel for a destination wedding?
faq.a: No one has to. Ask early, talk openly about who covers travel and time off, and make it easy for a friend to decline and still come as a guest.
